opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the more interesting and underappreciated parts of the Chinese AI story. In the U.S., so much of the conversation centers on frontier labs selling API access or consumer chat products. In China, the business reality is quite different. Enterprise software spending has historically been lower, companies are more reluctant to pay for SaaS, and there's a strong preference for on-premise or private deployments, especially in state-owned enterprises, finance, and government-adjacent sectors.

That shapes how B2B AI partnerships work. Much of the value goes to whoever can do the integration: customize a model, deploy it on local hardware, and maintain it. That favors the big cloud players like Alibaba, Baidu, Tencent, and Huawei, which already have enterprise relationships and infrastructure. It's less a "sell tokens through an API" business and more a systems-integration business.

Open-weight models change that dynamic a lot. When DeepSeek, Qwen, and others release very strong open models, the model itself becomes partly commoditized, and the competition moves to deployment, fine-tuning, and support. That's good for adoption, since lots of enterprises can now run capable models in-house, but it puts real pressure on margins for anyone trying to sell the model as the product. Price wars on inference in China have already been brutal.

The other big factor is compute. Export controls make access to top-end Nvidia hardware uncertain, so partnerships increasingly involve domestic chips. That creates friction in the short term, because the software ecosystems are less mature, but it may also produce a more vertically integrated domestic stack over time.

So my overall take: the prospects are real, and adoption will probably be broad, but it will look less like a few model companies capturing huge enterprise revenue and more like AI becoming a feature bundled into cloud, hardware, and integration deals. The winners will likely be the companies that already own the customer relationship and the infrastructure, not necessarily whoever has the single best model on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deployment preferences, integration, and margin pressure, but does not identify loss of control from relying on an external AI partner as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response describes systems integration and enterprise relationships, but does not question whether Chinese companies would welcome external forward-deployed engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest up front: China's B2B AI landscape isn't my primary area, so take this as the view of someone who studies the open model ecosystem and watches how it ripples outward.

With that caveat, I'm fairly optimistic, and the reason is mostly structural. The most interesting thing that happened in open models over the last couple of years is that Chinese labs, Qwen, DeepSeek, and a handful of others, became the default foundation for a huge share of the world's open-weight deployments. When you're a company in China trying to build an AI product for other businesses, you have strong, permissively licensed base models sitting right there, in your language, tuned for your market, and you don't have to route through an American API. That lowers the cost of forming a partnership enormously, because the hard part isn't the model anymore. It's the data, the integration, and the trust between two companies.

The second thing is that the Chinese enterprise market has always been more willing to do deep customization than the US market. A lot of US B2B AI is "call the API, wrap it, ship." In China you see more fine-tuning, more on-premise deployment, more vertical-specific models, partly because of data regulations and partly because that's how the software industry there has historically worked. That plays to the strengths of open weights.

Where I'd be cautious is on the economics. Margins on inference in China are brutal, the price wars among the big model providers have pushed per-token costs to nearly nothing, and that makes it hard for a middle layer of B2B partners to capture value. So I think the volume of partnerships will be very high, but the question of who actually makes money is still unresolved. The companies that win will be the ones that own something proprietary, whether that's data, distribution, or a workflow the customer can't easily replace, rather than the ones competing on model quality alone.

And the last factor is compute. Export controls make the hardware picture uncertain, and that affects how ambitious any partnership can be in training versus just inference. My guess is that this pushes even more energy into efficient open models and clever deployment, which honestly is where a lot of the innovation has been coming from anyway.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trust, data, integration, and inference economics, but does not identify loss of control from relying on an external AI partner as an obstacle.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the opportunity from the difficulty of executing on it. There’s a clear business case for partnerships where one company brings AI capabilities and another brings customers, domain expertise, and a way to integrate the technology into daily work. The question is whether that combination delivers something customers will actually pay for.

For China specifically, I’d be cautious about making a sweeping prediction—I don’t have enough firsthand visibility into those deals. I’d look at who can access the data, who owns the customer relationship, and who takes responsibility when the system makes a mistake. For cross-border partnerships, you also have regulatory and geopolitical uncertainty.

So I think there’s potential, but I’d be more optimistic about a narrow partnership that solves a measurable business problem than a broad announcement about two companies working together on AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the potential from the difficulty of building a durable business. There’s a clear opportunity for AI companies to partner with businesses that already have customers, distribution, and an understanding of a particular industry. But getting a model into a demo is very different from getting it into a workflow that someone will consistently pay for.

For China specifically, I’d want to understand who owns the customer relationship, how the partners handle data, and what each side brings that the other can’t easily replace. If your contribution is just access to a model, that’s a pretty fragile partnership. If you’re helping solve a specific operational problem and you can measure the improvement, that’s much more compelling.

So I’m cautiously optimistic, but I wouldn’t treat B2B AI partnerships as one big category. The prospects depend a lot on the industry, the economics, and whether the partnership creates something more durable than a thin layer over a model.

r001.rationale: The response calls a partnership based only on model access fragile, but does not identify loss of control from depending on an external AI partner as an obstacle to companies accepting partnerships.
